results.authors: Thomalla G, Simonsen CZ, Boutitie F, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients with unknown time of onset and an acute DWI lesion without marked FLAIR hyperintensity (DWI-FLAIR mismatch), IV alteplase improved 90-day functional outcome compared with placebo.
results.title: MRI-guided thrombolysis for stroke with unknown time of onset (WAKE-UP)

results.authors: Ma H, Campbell BCV, Parsons MW, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients 4.5 to 9 hours from onset, or with wake-up stroke within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep, who had salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging (core under 70 mL, mismatch ratio above 1.2, mismatch volume above 10 mL) and no planned thrombectomy, IV alteplase increased excellent functional outcome at 90 days, with more symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage.
results.title: Thrombolysis guided by perfusion imaging up to 9 hours after onset of stroke (EXTEND)

results.authors: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al.
results.key_finding: For wake-up or unknown-onset stroke, IV thrombolysis is reasonable either with a DWI-positive, FLAIR-negative lesion, or within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep with salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging in patients not eligible for thrombectomy.
results.title: 2026 AHA/ASA guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke

output.summary: Two imaging pathways select wake-up or unknown-onset stroke patients for IV thrombolysis: a DWI-FLAIR mismatch (WAKE-UP), and, within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep in patients not eligible for thrombectomy, penumbral mismatch on automated perfusion imaging (EXTEND criteria: core under 70 mL, ratio above 1.2, mismatch above 10 mL). A FLAIR-positive lesion closes only the first pathway.

required_recommendations: Establish last known well (23:00 the previous evening, 9 hours 15 minutes before arrival at 08:15; even if her normal 03:00 bathroom visit is taken as last known well, it is 5 hours 15 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (9).

Thrombectomy: not indicated (no large vessel occlusion; the right M1 has a 40-50% stenosis without occlusion).

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for the atrial fibrillation documented on Holter (the 45-second episode meets the 30-second definition of AF, and anticoagulation after stroke does not depend on AF burden; CHA2DS2-VASc 5; HAS-BLED 2 once aspirin is stopped; only one dose-reduction criterion, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, so no reduction) within 48 hours, since the 2.1 cm deep infarct is moderate in size without hemorrhagic transformation; stop aspirin, do not add an antiplatelet and do not bridge with heparin.
Intensify lipid lowering for the intracranial atherosclerosis (LDL 132 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 20 mg): add ezetimibe 10 mg and escalate further if LDL stays at or above 70 mg/dL.

Treat the other vascular risk factors: smoking cessation, CPAP adherence for obstructive sleep apnea, glycemic control (HbA1c 7.9%), and resumption of amlodipine and losartan after the first 48 to 72 hours with a long-term blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
NIHSS 9: gaze 1, visual 1 (visual extinction), facial palsy 1, left arm 1, left leg 1, sensory 1, dysarthria 1, extinction and inattention 2 (visual and tactile).

Wake-up stroke: FLAIR is positive, so the DWI-FLAIR limb is closed; the sleep midpoint is 02:45, 5 hours 30 minutes before arrival, and the patient is not an EVT candidate (no large vessel occlusion), so the perfusion limb applies, but CTP does not meet EXTEND criteria (core 2 mL, mismatch 1 mL, ratio 1.5).
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Subcortical (corona radiata) infarcts can be lacunar OR embolic to a single perforator — vessel imaging and cardiac evaluation are required to assign mechanism reliably

Inpatient Holter: paroxysmal AF (one 45-second episode, burden below 0.1%). CHA2DS2-VASc 5 (hypertension, diabetes, stroke 2, female sex); HAS-BLED 3 on aspirin (uncontrolled hypertension, stroke, antiplatelet), 2 once aspirin is stopped.
DWI-FLAIR mismatch on MRI is the tissue clock for wake-up presentations
CKD stage 3b (creatinine 1.5 mg/dL) does not justify delaying or replacing CTA in an acute stroke; the CTA does not wait for creatinine.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

clinical_pearls: Wake-up strokes account for approximately 20-25% of all ischemic strokes and require imaging-based selection for thrombolysis: DWI-FLAIR mismatch, or perfusion mismatch within 9 hours of the sleep midpoint when thrombectomy is not an option

The distinction between antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy for secondary prevention is one of the most consequential decisions in stroke management

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lucia Mendoza is a 58-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease stage 3b who presents to the emergency department after waking up at approximately 06:30 this morning with slurred speech and difficulty using her left hand. She reports going to bed at approximately 23:00 last night feeling entirely normal. She woke once around 03:00 to use the bathroom and states she felt fine at that time, though she acknowledges she was groggy and did not perform any fine motor tasks. When she woke at 06:30 for work, she noticed her speech sounded thick and her left hand was clumsy when she tried to button her shirt. She initially attributed this to sleeping on her arm but became concerned when the symptoms persisted after thirty minutes. She drove herself to a nearby urgent care center, which immediately redirected her to our emergency department via ambulance. EMS noted mild dysarthria, subtle left facial droop, and mild left upper extremity weakness on initial evaluation and activated a stroke alert. Fingerstick glucose in the field was 142 mg/dL. The patient arrived in the ED at 08:15. She denies any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting, seizure activity, or loss of consciousness. She reports no recent illness, fever, chest pain, or palpitations. She has been compliant with her medications but admits her blood pressure is often elevated when checked at the pharmacy. She also acknowledges that she has not been using her CPAP machine for the past several months because it makes her uncomfortable. Her last known well time is conservatively estimated at 23:00 the prior evening, approximately 9 hours and 15 minutes before ED arrival. Her self-reported bathroom visit at 03:00 raises the possibility that symptoms began after that time, though this cannot be confirmed.
